account: It is eight o'clock on day 1, and I am in my office with the secretary for morning business. I have read today's appointment book and both briefing books and returned them to their chest. The most unusual matter is that our ten o'clock grain inspection at the east-bank mill is still unconfirmed: the secretary found nobody there last evening or this morning. The baker and innkeeper did not know who manages its records, and freight had not answered before the secretary left. I do not know why staff were unavailable; this alone is not evidence of wrongdoing or a shortage. The inspection remains scheduled. Its purpose is to review grain stocks, delivery records, shortages, and storage concerns; we have not requested any supplies be moved. The secretary has offered to review correspondence now. My remaining appointments are lunch at home at noon, council letters in the office at thirteen, tea at fifteen with the neighbour at the dockside cottage by (16, -60, 105), office again at sixteen-thirty, and home at nineteen. Yesterday's tea was quiet, and the neighbour reported the baker busy with fresh loaves. I have no confirmed news of any other unusual town activity.
